title: A photonic integrated comb engine for ultracold quantum gases
authors: Wei Sun, Xiaoying Yan, Jinbao Long, Sanli Huang, Zhixin Duan, Zhenyuan Shang, Zeying Zhong, Jiahao Sun, Yue Hu, Shichang Li, Baoqi Shi, Yi-Han Luo, Shuyi Li, Hao Tan, Chen Shen, Zhichuan Niu, Shengjun Yang, Junqiu Liu
abstract: Cold atoms underpin quantum sensing, simulation and computation, but their coherent control demands highly stable optical fields whose generation, referencing and power scaling remain formidable integration challenges. While photonic integrated circuits have yielded compact visible lasers and high-$Q$ microresonators have enabled chip-scale optical frequency combs, these crucial technologies have largely remained functionally fragmented. Consequently, the coherent manipulation of ultracold quantum gases using a fully integrated laser-comb source has yet to be realized. Here we demonstrate a scalable, hybrid-integrated microcomb engine at 780 nm that seamlessly bridges frequency synthesis, atomic referencing and power amplification to achieve quantum state control of a Bose--Einstein condensate. By self-injection locking of electrically driven III--V lasers to high-$Q$ Si$_3$N$_4$ microresonators, we generate coherent platicon microcombs featuring 20- and 100-GHz mode spacings. Absolute referencing of the microcomb to an $^{85}$Rb transition actively suppresses long-term frequency drift from over 200 MHz to the 100-kHz level across 2,000 s. A selected comb tooth is subsequently injection-amplified to 102 mW, entirely preserving the microcomb's pristine coherence and stability. We utilize this synthesized field to construct an optical lattice, drive coherent two-photon Raman transitions, and prepare stationary spin-orbit-coupled and Raman-lattice states within an $^{87}$Rb condensate. By providing a synchronized optical grid, this atom-referenced microcomb allows multiple optical-control channels to scale without a proportional multiplication of independent frequency references. Our work establishes a transformative, fully integrated frequency-synthesis architecture essential for realizing deployable, large-scale atomic quantum systems.
summary: The research presents a fully integrated, scalable microcomb engine that solves the major challenge of generating stable optical fields for quantum gas experiments. By combining microresonator physics, laser stabilization, and atomic referencing, they achieve a highly stable light source capable of controlling quantum states in Bose-Einstein condensates.
main_problem: Coherently controlling ultracold quantum gases requires highly stable optical fields, but generating, referencing, and scaling these fields remains a formidable integration challenge.
main_result: The authors demonstrated a scalable, hybrid-integrated microcomb engine that successfully provides a synchronized optical grid for controlling quantum states in an ultracold Bose-Einstein condensate.
method: The system uses self-injection locking of III-V lasers into Si3N4 microresonators to generate a microcomb, which is then actively referenced to an atomic transition and amplified for use in lattice/Raman interactions.
model_or_system: The platform is a photonic integrated comb engine operating at 780 nm, designed for Bose-Einstein condensates of Rb atoms. It integrates frequency synthesis (microcomb generation), atomic referencing, and power amplification into one chip-scale module.
key_observables: Frequency stability (suppressing drift from >200 MHz to 100 kHz over 2,000 s), mode spacings (20- and 100-GHz), and successful preparation of spin-orbit-coupled and Raman-lattice states.
important_parameters: 780 nm wavelength, 102 mW amplified power, and the ability to scale multiple optical control channels from a single reference source.
main_assumptions: The work establishes a transformative, fully integrated frequency-synthesis architecture, implying previous methods were functionally fragmented.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the integrated setup, comb generation via SIL, cold-atom manipulation showing optical lattices and Raman coupling, and comparisons highlighting SWaP-C advantages.
paper_structure: The paper details the generation of the microcomb via SIL on Si3N4 resonators, followed by active referencing to an atomic transition (MTS), subsequent amplification, and finally, the application of this stable field to create and manipulate quantum states in an ultracold gas.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the engineering bottleneck in quantum simulation by providing a robust, chip-scale source of highly stable, multi-frequency light necessary for complex quantum control protocols.
